newsitem.title: CHINA: China says no change yet at top of stock markets.
newsitem.headline: China says no change yet at top of stock markets.

text.p: China has not reshuffled the heads of its two stock markets, exchange officials said, and officials of China's top watchdog body said on Friday they knew nothing about personnel changes.

However, brokers said such a reshuffle could not be ruled out, especially after the appointment of a new chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commmission (CSRC). Zhou Zhengqing, former head of the Securities Commission under the State Council, or cabinet, took over the CSRC this month.

Hong Kong's Ming Bao newspaper reported on Friday that Beijing had appointed Tu Guangshao, formerly in charge of the transactions department at the CSRC, to take over as head of the Shanghai stock market.
Gui Minjie, currently head of the international department of the CSRC, would move to take charge of the Shenzhen stock market, it said.
"We know nothing about this," a CSRC spokesman said.
Yang Xianghai continued to hold the post of president of the Shanghai stock exchange, a Shanghai exchange official said.
"We have received no notification of a personnel change," the official said.
Asked if Shenzhen exchange president Zhuang Xinyi had been replaced, an exchange official said he did not know.
"The replacement of a stock exchange head is a subject for the CSRC," the Shenzhen official said, adding that Zhuang was on a business trip overseas.
Brokers said such a reshuffle was to be expected.

"The change would be quite normal because the chairman of the CSRC has been replaced," an official at China Guotai Securities in Shenzhen told the Hong Kong-based China Securities Bulletin. "It would be the turn to replace the heads of the stock exchanges. This would strengthen (Beijing's) authority.
"The CSRC wants to directly control the exchanges this time," he said. "The autonomy of stock exchanges would be eroded by a reshuffle.
Analysts played down the impact of such a shake-up on the markets.
"It will only benefit the market because Beijing wants to see a healthier market as well as a tamed market," a Shenzhen analyst with China Securities Co told the China Securities Bulletin.
